extracted.intended_audience: readers of satirical fiction and critics of educational/social institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted norms and evaluative practices described within a satirical Victorian novel (Erewhon) that portray how students, scholarship, art, and invention are judged in that fictional society. Useful for analysing fictional prescriptions about pedagogy, examinations, and cultural values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence of hypothetics study
rubrics_metrics.description: The main feature in their system is the prominence which they give to a study which I can only translate by the word 'hypothetics.' They require youths to imagine utterly strange and impossible contingencies and give intelligent answers, and the hypothetical language is taught for many of their best years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothetics is valued as preparation for extraordinary contingencies; proficiency is highly rewarded (even maintenance for life). Institutions spend years on translating good poetry into the hypothetical language; fluency is 'a distinguishing mark of a scholar and a gentleman.' The narrator criticises this as a waste when practical problems remain unsolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development of unreason (Professorships of Inconsistency and Evasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: They have professorships of Inconsistency and Evasion intended to develop 'unreasoning faculties' required for daily conduct; youths are examined in these subjects before being allowed to proceed to hypothetics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are trained to defend glaring inconsistencies and to find pretexts for disregarding injunctions; the more conscientious attain surprising proficiency. Unreason is justified as the complement of reason and necessary to avoid the absurd extremes of strict logical deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage competition; no class lists
rubrics_metrics.description: They have no class lists and discourage anything like competition among the students; competition is regarded as self-seeking and unneighbourly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examinations are conducted so as to avoid fostering rivalry: emphasis is on conformity and social harmony rather than ranking students. The cultural norm punishes self-seeking behaviour and prizes mediocrity as socially stabilising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination design: set papers (some known, some unknown)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examinations are conducted by way of papers written by the candidate on set subjects, some known beforehand, while others are devised to test general capacity and savoir faire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mixture is meant to probe both prepared knowledge and adaptive cleverness. The narrator recounts an example where an examiner deliberately planted errors in a published article and then set a paper to test whether students would repeat those blunders, resulting in many being 'plucked.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Desired answer traits: vagueness, qualifying language, distrust of printed matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are expected to exhibit vagueness and a certain distrust of received opinion; examples given include plucking a student for 'want of sufficient vagueness,' refusing a degree for being too often 'in the right,' and rejecting work for insufficient distrust of printed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answers that deploy qualifying adverbs ('carefully,' 'patiently,' 'earnestly') and that avoid rigid definiteness are rewarded. Excessive correctness, directness, or unquestioning acceptance of printed sources are penalised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of originality and genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Of genius they make no account: every one is a genius more or less, and the institutions aim to ensure students 'think as we do' rather than to encourage independent thought; there is an active programme of suppressing 'useless knowledge' and obliterating the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The duty of senior scholars is framed as ensuring conformity; originality is equated to offence and is discouraged. Societies (e.g., 'Society for the Suppression of Useless Knowledge') and professors (e.g., President of the Society) exemplify institutionalised anti-originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress must be consensual and not outrun peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress is acceptable only if it 'commends itself to the common sense of the people' — a man who knows more than his neighbours should keep his knowledge until he can bring them with him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is regarded as immoral to be 'too far in front of one's own age'; intellectual advances must be paced to the community's readiness. The ideal is to avoid gratuitously telling people what they do not want to know.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art education: equal emphasis on commercial history and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Art courses are divided into the practical and the commercial; no student may continue practical study unless he makes equal progress in the commercial history — painters are examined in prices realised by leading pictures and value fluctuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The artist is treated as a dealer: understanding market values and adapting work to what will 'fetch' certain prices is as important as technical ability. Curriculum explicitly trains artists to suit market demands ('what kind of a picture will fetch how much').

rubrics_metrics.name: Social habit of avoiding expressed opinion (fear-of-giving-themselves-away)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a cultural disease of 'fear-of-giving-themselves-away' where people avoid definite opinions for fear of being exposed; scholarship prizes sitting 'gracefully on a fence' and retailing others' opinions with inscrutable caveats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Politeness consists in perpetual hedging: reviewers often argue opposite to their ostensible view, and it is expected that one 'suspects a hidden “yea” in every “nay”.' The ideal scholar avoids committing to clear positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examinations as social control (example of planted errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A professor authored an article full of plausible blunders, then set an exam allowing students to repeat those blunders (believing the article was by their examiner), subsequently plucking them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examinations are used not merely to test knowledge but to enforce conformity and to penalise intellectual credulity or insufficient distrust. This demonstrates an evaluative practice that values suspicion of authority and punishes uncritical acceptance.
